chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Al-Amraki ibn Ali, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him), said:

I asked him about a man who had a nosebleed and cleared it by blowing, so some of that blood became small pieces and hit his water container. Is it valid for him to perform wudu from it? He said: If there is nothing apparent in the water, there is no problem; but if there is something apparent, he should not perform wudu from it.
He said: And I asked him about a man who had a nosebleed while he was performing wudu, so a drop dripped into his water container. Is the wudu valid from it? He said: No.
ai.seo_question: Does a nosebleed invalidate wudu if blood mixes with the water?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the distinction between minor impurity (najāsah khafīfah) and major impurity in water used for wudu, emphasizing the criterion of visible discernibility (istibān) for blood fragments. It further establishes that direct contamination during the act of wudu invalidates the ritual, reflecting the Shia juristic principle that the state of the water at the moment of use determines validity. This ruling underscores the practical application of purity laws in daily worship, ensuring that ritual cleanliness is maintained without undue hardship.
